newsitem.title: UK: UK back on course to meet PSBR target - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK back on course to meet PSBR target - analysts.

text.p: A record repayment of government debt in October dispelled fears of overshooting public debt this year, and made it easier for Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to justify tax cuts in his forthcoming budget, economists said.
Data from the ONS showed a net repayment of 4.4 billion stg into government coffers in October, bringing the cumulative PSBR to 11.4 bln stg, versus 18.7 bln in the same period last year.
"This makes Clarke's life easier in terms of persuading that tax cuts are justified," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist James Barty.
"It allows him more opportunity for pleasing the electorate with tax cuts and pleasing the gilts market with a downwards revision to future PSBR figures," he added.
Budget forecasters largely expect the Chancellor to find room for around three billion sterling in tax cuts next Tuesday.
Economists said the jump in the PSDR was due to a sharp surge in tax receipts, particularly corporation tax, which was up 24.5 percent on last year.
"The only question is how much January's corporation tax payment will be reduced correspondingly due to today's figure," said Peter Warburton, chief economist at Robert Fleming.
"The PSBR is probably going to undershoot its target this year," he said, adding he would likely revise his forecast for the 1996/97 PSBR to 25-25.5 bln stg from a previous forecast of 26.5 bln.
In the summer, the Chancellor forecast a 26.9 billion stg borrowing requirement for 1996/97.
Clarke is under pressure from his back-benchers to deliver tax cuts in his November 26 budget to sweeten voters ahead of the general election which must be held by May next year.
"The data clearly relaxes the Chancellor's hands ahead of the budget," said General Accident economist Andrew Milligan.
Economists said the other downside to Monday's data was the rebound in departmental spending growth to 22.4 billion stg, up 7.3 percent on October last year.
"But any overshoot on spending this year looks set to be offset by higher-than-forecast receipts growth," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
The other side of the coin to strong tax receipts is concern about runaway growth and inflation, some economists said.
"The much larger than expected debt repayment also argues against any tax cuts in the upcoming budget," said Bank America senior economic adivser Jeremy Hawkins.

"Very strong tax receipts, especially out of the corporate sector, provide additional evidence of the buoyancy of the economy at the start of the quarter and hence, the lack of and need for further stimulus," he added.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Barty said the worry in the run up to the budget was a small-scale repetition of the mistakes of the 1980s when then Chancellor Nigel Lawson cut taxes as the economy was acclerating, prompting the late 1980s boom.
"That is a worry, but I think Clarke will come out with a budget which will at least try to finance tax cuts with spending cuts. Today's number makes it a bit easier for him," Barty said.
